Pronunciation note for this grammar point:
The particle is stressed when it carries the meaning: call it OFF, the plan fell THROUGH. In three-part verbs the middle word is weak.
Read it aloud, then record yourself: the main stress falls on the content word, not on the hedge.

elements.content: Grammar focus: Phrasal Verbs: Extended Patterns.

Learn the pattern with the verb, then the register. In a report, replace the phrasal verb with its single-word equivalent: postpone for put off, tolerate for put up with, investigate for look into. In speech, the phrasal verb is the natural choice, and the Latinate verb sounds stiff.

separable — object before or after the particle: call off the meeting / call the meeting off
pronoun with separable — always between: call it off
inseparable — particle stays with the verb: look after the file
three-part — inseparable, gerund after to: put up with the delay, look forward to hearing
intransitive — no object at all: the plan fell through
register — single Latinate verb in formal writing: postpone, tolerate, investigate
Guided practice: choose the correct option.
1. Which is correct?
2. Complete: 'I look forward to ___ from you.'
3. Which verb is three-part?
Read and listen: three examples in context.

They called off the meeting. — Separable: particle after the object too. (Call the meeting off.)
The plan fell through. — Intransitive: no object. (Nothing separates.)
They put up with the delay. — Three-part: inseparable. (Put up with something.)
What do you observe?

Phrasal verbs come in three patterns. Separable verbs take the object between verb and particle, or after it: call off the meeting, call the meeting off, but a pronoun must sit between (call it off). Inseparable verbs keep the particle next to the verb: look after the file, never look the file after. Three-part verbs (put up with, get away with, look forward to) are inseparable and take the gerund after to.
1. Where must a pronoun go with a separable verb?
options: Between the verb and the particle.

elements.content: 2. What follows look forward to?
State the rule in one sentence, without looking at the table.
Freer production: I can talk about everyday situations with common phrasal verbs.

Success criteria:
- I can tell a separable from an inseparable phrasal verb.
- I can put a pronoun in the right place.
- I can replace a phrasal verb with a formal equivalent.
Role play: put your position in ninety seconds; your partner notes every use of the target structure.
Frequent errors and correction:

❌ They called off it (pronoun after the particle of a separable verb) → ✅ They called it off
❌ She looks the archive after (inseparable verb split by its object) → ✅ She looks after the archive
Correct these sentences: say what is wrong, then give the right version.
Acceptable variants:

They put the launch off until June.
She looks after the archive.
We will not put up with further delays.

- Professional audience: transpose the structure into a memo.
- Academic audience: transpose it into a paragraph of analysis.
